Backyard play turf for Hunters Creek's second-generation families

Playground turf in Hunters Creek runs $10–$25 per square foot as of September 2026, priced by pad thickness and the fall height of whatever equipment sits on top. Many of the community's original 1990s buyers have been replaced by a second generation of young families filling the same swing sets and jungle gyms, and a cushioned surface under that equipment is one of the few turf jobs the association reviews under the same enclosed-back-yard rule as a full lawn.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a 300 sq ft play area behind a swing set

Say you have a 300 sq ft play area planned behind a swing set and a small climbing structure in a fenced Villanova back yard, sized for a seven-foot fall height on the tallest platform. At the published $10–$25 per sq ft range, that area prices between $3,000 and $7,500 installed, typically $12–$19: about $3,600 to $5,700 for the full 300 sq ft, with pad thickness under the platform driving most of the difference between the low and high end.

A community built for kids, now filling with a second generation

Hunters Creek's villages went in mostly between the late 1980s and the early 2000s, and three decades later many of the original swing sets and play structures have been replaced once already, sometimes twice, as homes changed hands to families with young children again. The community's recreation amenities, ball fields, a playground and courts near the clubhouse, reflect that same family orientation, but a backyard play area is still where most of the daily use actually happens. Turf under a home play structure holds up to that kind of repeated, concentrated traffic in a way grass under a swing set rarely does past the first year.

Where rubber infill is actually allowed

Florida's turf standard keeps rubber and other synthetic infill off a Hunters Creek lawn, pet run, or putting green entirely, restricting those areas to silica sand, zeolite, or a coated sand instead. Equipment fall zones get a specific carve-out from that same rule: the ground directly beneath a swing set or climbing structure is allowed to use rubber or another engineered infill product, since that material does cushioning work the natural-material options weren't built for. The line between the two infill categories is drawn at the equipment's footprint itself, not at the edge of the play area as a whole, which matters if a project blends turf types across one yard.

Why a front-yard play set still needs natural grass here

The HCCA's turf review only covers an enclosed rear yard, which matters for any family whose play structure sits in view of the street rather than behind a fence. A front-yard play area has to stay on natural sod from the association's approved list, kept under six inches, since the guideline doesn't extend its case-by-case turf review to a front lot at all. That's not a state or county rule, just this one association's own line between what gets reviewed and what doesn't, worth checking before pricing a play area that isn't actually in the back yard.

Why a play area needs a deeper base than a lawn

Excavation for a Hunters Creek play area has to account for three layers stacking on top of each other, the compacted rock, the shock pad, and the turf itself, which is why the hole goes noticeably deeper than a lawn conversion covering the same square footage. Shortchanging that depth calculation is what leaves a finished play surface sitting visibly higher than the grass around it, and that mismatch creates its own trip hazard right at the edge even when every layer above the rock was installed correctly. Working out the full stack's thickness on paper before any soil comes out avoids discovering the shortfall halfway through the job.

What retrofitting a playground into an old lawn can strike underground

Removing an established Hunters Creek lawn's turf and shallow base to make room for a deeper playground system risks hitting a capped irrigation line that served that section before the original lawn conversion, since a line with nothing connected to it years later doesn't always get flagged during a quick site walk. Digging into one unexpectedly during a retrofit's deeper excavation can mean an unplanned repair on a section of pipe that technically isn't even doing anything anymore. Checking old valve box records or asking whoever handled the original lawn work avoids that surprise before the first shovel of a retrofit project.

The final walk-through before handing off a play surface

The last step on a Hunters Creek playground project is infilling at the manufacturer's specified rate, then walking the finished surface to check for flat, even coverage and confirm nothing shifted during the last stages of the build. This walk-through is where a crew catches a low spot, an uneven seam, or a containment edge that needs a final adjustment before calling the job finished. Skipping this check and assuming a play surface is ready just because the visible steps are done is how small problems make it to the first day of use instead of getting caught beforehand.

Rinsing a play surface before kids go out in summer

A hose rinse timed just before outdoor play begins can pull a Hunters Creek play surface's temperature down 30 to 50 degrees in a matter of minutes, and building that step into a summer routine matters here in a way it doesn't for a lawn nobody sits on directly. Rinsing ahead of an afternoon play window, rather than waiting until the surface already feels uncomfortably hot underfoot, keeps the worst of the afternoon heat from ever becoming an issue in the first place. It's one of the simplest habits on this list and among the most worth keeping consistent through the hottest months.

Sizing the pad to the equipment, not just the yard

A shock pad under playground turf gets sized to the fall height of the specific equipment sitting on it, not a flat number that works for every swing set, and on a modest pool-cage-era lot the play area itself is often the main constraint on layout rather than square footage. Florida's turf standard allows rubber infill only within the footprint of the play equipment; the ground outside that footprint, if it's turfed at all, goes back to the same silica or coated-sand infill a lawn would use. What the material standard covers for kids goes through the rest of that rule.

Questions people ask

Can playground turf go around a swing set that's already installed?

Yes, most jobs build the pad and turf around existing equipment rather than requiring it to come down first, though the footings sometimes need temporary support during excavation.

Does a play area need the same ARC drainage note as a lawn?

Yes, since the association reviews it as artificial turf either way; the note should also flag where infill differs, rubber under the fall zone, standard infill everywhere else on the turfed area.
